questions.text: A pilot is flying a Cessna 172 certificated in the Normal category. Can this aircraft be intentionally spun?

options.label: A
options.text: No. Normal category aircraft are explicitly NOT approved for intentional spins. They are only tested by the manufacturer to ensure that if a 1-turn inadvertent spin occurs, the aircraft can recover within one additional turn without exceeding structural limits. Intentional spins in a Normal category aircraft risk entering a multi-turn spin that may flatten and become unrecoverable as the rudder becomes blanked by the fuselage and wing wake.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, as long as the aircraft is within published weight and balance limits and the pilot holds a current medical certificate.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, but only if a CFI is on board. The parachute exemption under 91.307(d)(2) authorizes spins in any aircraft when given by a CFI.

options.label: D
options.text: No, because spins exceed the structural G-limits of all Normal category aircraft. The spin forces would damage the airframe.

questions.explanation: Normal category aircraft are tested for inadvertent spin recovery only (1 turn + 1 turn to recover). They are NOT approved for intentional spins. The 91.307(d)(2) parachute exemption (Option C) applies to the parachute requirement, NOT to the aircraft category limitation — you still cannot intentionally spin a Normal category aircraft. Option D is incorrect — spins don't necessarily exceed G-limits; the issue is recoverability, not structural failure.

questions.text: How can a pilot distinguish between a spin and a spiral dive?

options.label: A
options.text: Check the airspeed indicator. In a TRUE SPIN, the airspeed is LOW and STABLE — the massive drag of the stalled wings acts like a parachute, preventing acceleration. The indicated airspeed will hover near the published stall speed. In a SPIRAL DIVE, the wings are NOT stalled. The aircraft is accelerating in a descending turn, and the airspeed increases RAPIDLY toward Vne. This distinction is critical because the recovery procedures are opposite: spin recovery requires reducing AOA (PARE), while spiral dive recovery requires reducing bank angle and power.

options.label: B
options.text: In a spin, the aircraft is inverted. In a spiral dive, the aircraft is right-side up.

options.label: C
options.text: In a spin, the engine is at full power. In a spiral dive, the engine is at idle.

options.label: D
options.text: Spins and spiral dives are the same maneuver at different altitudes. The recovery procedure is identical for both.

questions.explanation: The airspeed indicator is the primary diagnostic. Spin = low airspeed, stable (wings stalled, massive drag). Spiral dive = high airspeed, increasing rapidly (wings not stalled, aircraft accelerating). Applying spin recovery (PARE) to a spiral dive would be incorrect — a spiral dive requires power reduction, level wings, and smooth pull-out. Applying spiral dive recovery to a spin would be equally incorrect. Option B is wrong — spins are not necessarily inverted. Option D conflates two fundamentally different aerodynamic states.

questions.text: An aircraft enters a spin at 3,000 feet AGL. The pilot freezes for 3 full turns before beginning recovery. Approximately how much altitude has been lost, and is recovery still possible?

options.label: A
options.text: Approximately 1,500 feet (about 500 feet per turn). The aircraft is now at approximately 1,500 feet AGL. Recovery IS still possible but URGENT — the PARE procedure will take at least 0.5 to 1 additional turn to stop rotation (another 250-500 feet), plus the dive pull-out requires 200-500 feet. Total altitude needed from this point: approximately 500-1,000 feet. At 1,500 AGL, there is enough altitude IF the pilot acts immediately with proper, full-deflection PARE inputs. Any further delay reduces the margin to zero.

options.label: B
options.text: Approximately 300 feet total. Spins descend slowly because the stalled wings create high drag. Recovery is easily achievable with ample altitude remaining.

options.label: C
options.text: Approximately 3,000 feet. The aircraft has impacted the ground because spins descend at terminal velocity.

options.label: D
options.text: The altitude loss cannot be estimated because spin descent rates vary unpredictably. The pilot should simply execute PARE and hope for the best.

questions.explanation: The standard estimate is approximately 500 feet per turn for typical GA aircraft. Three turns ≈ 1,500 feet lost. From 3,000 AGL to approximately 1,500 AGL, recovery is tight but achievable — if the pilot acts immediately with proper inputs. From lower entry altitudes (e.g., 800 AGL in the pattern), 1.5 turns = 750 feet, leaving essentially no altitude for recovery + pull-out. Option B drastically underestimates the descent rate. Option C overestimates. Option D is defeatist — altitude loss is predictable enough to plan recovery margins.

questions.text: During the 'R' step of PARE, the pilot applies full opposite rudder and the rotation slows, then stops. The pilot continues holding full opposite rudder. What happens next?

options.label: A
options.text: The aircraft enters a CROSSOVER SPIN in the opposite direction. Once the original rotation stops, the full opposite rudder that arrested the first spin now becomes a PRO-SPIN input for the opposite direction. The rudder creates a strong yawing moment, and if the wings are still stalled (elevator has not yet been pushed forward in the 'E' step, or the pull-out is aggressive), the aircraft snaps into autorotation in the new direction. The pilot must IMMEDIATELY neutralize the rudder the moment rotation stops, then proceed to the elevator step to break the stall.

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing — holding opposite rudder after the spin stops simply keeps the aircraft yawed. The rudder must be held until the aircraft is in level flight to prevent re-entering the original spin.

options.label: C
options.text: The aircraft will enter a spiral dive in the opposite direction. The increased airspeed from the spin recovery makes a crossover spin impossible.

options.label: D
options.text: The aircraft will immediately return to level flight. The opposite rudder, combined with the natural stability of the aircraft, provides a self-correcting recovery.

questions.explanation: The crossover spin is a real and dangerous phenomenon. After the original rotation stops, full opposite rudder becomes a pro-spin yawing moment for the other direction. If the wings are still stalled (the pilot hasn't completed the 'E' step yet), the conditions for a spin in the new direction are present: stall + yaw. The pilot must neutralize the rudder the MOMENT rotation stops. Option B is dangerous advice — it would directly cause a crossover spin. Option C is incorrect — crossover spins are well-documented in spin testing.

questions.text: In the PARE procedure, why is the 'A' (Ailerons Neutral) step included? Why can't the pilot use ailerons to stop the rotation?

options.label: A
options.text: In a spin, both wings are stalled. If the pilot applies aileron to 'roll out' of the spin (e.g., right aileron in a left spin), the LEFT aileron deflects DOWNWARD. This increases the camber and effectively increases the local angle of attack on the already deeply stalled left wing. A deeper stall on the left wing means even LESS lift and even MORE drag on that side, which ACCELERATES the autorotation rather than stopping it. Ailerons are effective roll control devices only when the wings are NOT stalled and airflow is attached. During a stall, ailerons worsen the asymmetry. They must remain neutral until the stall is broken.

options.label: B
options.text: Ailerons are neutral because deflecting them during a spin risks structural failure. The forces on the ailerons during autorotation exceed the wing's design limits.

options.label: C
options.text: Ailerons are neutral because they are aerodynamically ineffective during a spin. They don't help, but they also don't hurt.

options.label: D
options.text: Ailerons are neutral because the pilot needs both hands free to apply full rudder force. Spin recovery requires maximum physical force on the rudder pedals.

questions.explanation: Ailerons during a spin actively WORSEN the autorotation by increasing the AOA on the pro-spin (dropping) wing. This is not 'ineffective' (Option C) — it is actively harmful. The downward aileron increases camber and local AOA on a wing that is already past the critical AOA, deepening the stall and increasing drag, which accelerates the yaw and roll into the spin. Option B is incorrect — the forces don't exceed structural limits, but the aerodynamic effect is destructive to recovery. Option D is physically wrong — rudder is controlled by feet.

questions.text: Why does the 'P' (Power to Idle) step come FIRST in the PARE procedure?

options.label: A
options.text: Engine power is a pro-spin force in multiple ways. (1) The propeller slipstream accelerates airflow over the horizontal stabilizer, increasing the downward force on the tail, which pushes the nose UP and FLATTENS the spin. A flat spin blanks the rudder behind the fuselage and wing wake, potentially making recovery impossible. (2) Gyroscopic precession of the spinning propeller can accelerate the spin rate. (3) The torque reaction from the engine adds a rolling moment. Cutting power to idle immediately removes ALL of these pro-spin forces before the pilot attempts to use the rudder to break the autorotation.

options.label: B
options.text: Power is cut to reduce airspeed. Lower airspeed makes the aircraft easier to control during the recovery.

options.label: C
options.text: Power is cut to prevent the engine from overstressing during the high rotational forces of the spin. Engine mounts can fail under spin G-loads.

options.label: D
options.text: Power is cut because the propeller creates turbulence that interferes with the rudder's ability to generate anti-spin yaw. Removing power clears the airflow over the tail.

questions.explanation: Power has three distinct pro-spin effects: (1) slipstream flattens the spin by increasing tail-down force, (2) gyroscopic precession accelerates rotation, and (3) torque adds rolling moment. All three must be eliminated before rudder input can be effective. Option B is wrong — airspeed is already low in a spin, and reducing it further isn't the goal. Option C is wrong — engine mounts don't fail during spins. Option D is partially correct about airflow but misidentifies the primary mechanism (the issue is spin flattening, not turbulence interference).

questions.text: A CFI candidate is practicing intentional spins at 5,000 feet AGL in a Utility category aircraft. After 2 turns in a developed spin, the student applies the PARE procedure. The rotation slows but does not stop after 1 turn of recovery inputs. What should the student do?

options.label: A
options.text: Release all inputs and re-apply PARE from the beginning. The initial application may have had incorrect timing or insufficient rudder force. Start fresh: power idle, ailerons neutral, FULL opposite rudder (verify the correct direction), elevator briskly forward. Maintain the inputs and wait — some aircraft types require up to 2 full turns of anti-spin inputs before the rotation stops. If recovery is not achieved within 2 additional turns, the spin may be unrecoverable — deploy the ballistic parachute if equipped, or prepare for emergency egress.

options.label: B
options.text: Add full power to help 'blow' the aircraft out of the spin. More thrust will accelerate the aircraft enough to generate sufficient lift to break the stall.

options.label: C
options.text: Apply full aileron in the direction of the spin to try to 'overpower' the autorotation. If standard PARE didn't work, the student needs to use more aggressive control inputs.

options.label: D
options.text: Accept that the spin is unrecoverable and prepare for impact. Once PARE doesn't work on the first attempt, the aircraft is in a flat spin.

questions.sjt_rationale: Option B (impulsivity) adds power — the exact OPPOSITE of PARE step 1. Power flattens the spin and blanks the rudder. This will make recovery impossible. Option C (macho) applies aileron — the exact OPPOSITE of PARE step 2. This deepens the stall on the pro-spin wing and accelerates autorotation. Option D (resignation) gives up after one attempt — some aircraft genuinely require 2+ turns of anti-spin inputs. PARE is not instantaneous. Option A correctly restarts the procedure, verifies direction (common error: applying rudder in the wrong direction), and gives the physics time to work.
questions.explanation: PARE recovery is not always instantaneous, especially in a developed spin. Some aircraft require 1-2 full turns of sustained anti-spin inputs before the rotation stops. The most common reason PARE 'doesn't work' is insufficient rudder force, incorrect rudder direction, or inadvertent aileron input. Restarting the procedure with deliberate attention to each step is the correct response. At 5,000 AGL minus the altitude already lost (~1,000 ft for 2 developed turns), there is still adequate altitude for multiple recovery attempts.

questions.text: A pilot notices that during a power-on stall practice at 2,500 feet AGL, they forgot to apply right rudder. As the stall breaks, the aircraft yaws sharply to the left and the left wing drops aggressively. The aircraft begins to rotate. What is the pilot's FIRST action?

options.label: A
options.text: Apply full right aileron to pick up the dropped left wing. The stall has already broken, so normal roll control should be effective.

options.label: B
options.text: Recognize this as an incipient spin entry and IMMEDIATELY execute PARE: Power IDLE, Ailerons NEUTRAL, Rudder FULL RIGHT (opposite the left rotation), Elevator forward to break the stall. Act NOW — the incipient phase (first 1-2 turns) is the optimal recovery window. The autorotation is not yet locked in, and aggressive, correct anti-spin inputs will stop the rotation with minimal altitude loss. At 2,500 AGL, there is adequate altitude, but every second of delay costs ~500 feet.

options.label: C
options.text: Add full power to accelerate through the stall. The engine thrust will generate enough airflow over the wings to break the stall without needing to push the nose down.

options.label: D
options.text: Hold the current control inputs and wait for the aircraft to recover on its own. Certificated aircraft are designed to be naturally stable and will self-correct from a spin entry.

questions.sjt_rationale: Option A (impulsivity) applies aileron — which will deepen the stall on the dropping wing and accelerate the spin entry. Even if the stall has 'broken' on one wing, the dropped wing is still stalled (both wings are stalled in a spin, one just MORE than the other). Option C (macho) adds power — which flattens the spin. Full power is the last thing you want. Option D (invulnerability) assumes the aircraft will self-recover — Normal category aircraft are tested for inadvertent spin recovery, but the pilot should not rely on this and should actively recover immediately. Option B correctly identifies the incipient spin and executes PARE while the golden window is still open.
questions.explanation: The scenario describes a classic incipient spin entry: stall + yaw (from P-factor due to missing right rudder) → sharp left yaw → left wing drop → rotation begins. This is the INCIPIENT phase — the pilot has 1-2 turns (2-4 seconds) before the spin develops into a steady-state condition. PARE executed immediately in the incipient phase is highly effective and minimizes altitude loss. At 2,500 AGL, there is adequate margin, but prompt action is essential.
